AI services · The person behind the endpoint

Routstr adds Jev. The operator still matters.

The classifier can now be paid for in sats. In the discussion around its arrival, redshift spells out what users still have to trust about a provider.

A launch, a price claim and the work still ahead

Routstr announces that Jev is available through its service. The post describes a fast, inexpensive classifier, names the model as jev-latest and says it is live on one node at the time of the announcement. Access is through an updated routstrd client or the project’s SDK.

Redshift supplies the price pitch: A single sat can get you 20-50 requests. That is the provider’s stated rate, rather than a benchmark performed by this paper.

Juraj describes the attraction as a competitive market for model access: fund Routstr’s internal Cashu wallet over Lightning, then pay for calls without a subscription or credit card.

The reply underneath is more revealing than the launch slogan. Redshift explains that providers are currently enabled by redshift: Your routstrd (client) doesn't automatically pick up any Routstr node from Nostr.

Users can enable or disable nodes. In redshift’s account, they still trust a provider to serve the model it claims to serve, avoid logging requests and refrain from inserting hostile instructions. Automatic selection using information from Nostr is described as the eventual goal.

In a separate reply, redshift points to a public node-audit page. The discussion leaves two tasks visible: making access cheap enough to experiment with, and giving users grounds to choose the operator handling those experiments.

From the app desk

The browser keeps the keys

Team Soapbox’s listing for Tenna describes a browser for websites published to Nostr. A signed manifest identifies the files; the browser fetches them from Blossom, verifies them and serves the site locally.

The account boundary is the central promise: Tenna holds your keys; the sites never do.

The listing says signing requests pass through Tenna, with permissions remembered by site and event kind and revocable from its shield menu. Sites get separate origins and can be added from a catalogue, followed accounts or pasted Nostr identifiers.

Dispatches

Desktop tools

KindBeamer gets its own look

Juraj’s update to KindBeamer gives it an appearance inspired by e-ink, a website and an emphasis on keyboard navigation.

The announcement’s instruction is succinct: Better use with keyboard - everything has shortcuts.

Juraj describes the change as a move away from the look of Send to Kindle. The update is about how the tool feels to use, with shortcuts taking a more prominent role.

An invitation to other clients

Memories needn’t stay in one app

Seth says Zap Cooking’s memories feature is available on Android, iOS and the web, and invites other Nostr clients to build on it.

I’d love to see more clients take the open source code, build on the idea, and make #memories a standard across Nostr.

This is a call for adoption. Seth’s post identifies a working feature that other clients could reuse; it does not announce an agreed standard.

Funding privacy software

A €1,000 gift waits for a name

MetropleX asks the sender of a €1,000 GrapheneOS donation through Wise to make contact with their full name so the payment can be unfrozen. The post also reports smaller donations being returned.

In the ensuing discussion, MetropleX defends donors’ ability to choose their payment method: Part of freedom is allowing people the ability to choose for themselves.

The practical request is still to reach the donor. Nothing in these posts confirms that the held payment has been released.

After asking the network for prayers for their oldest child, Small Batch Steve reports that law enforcement made contact and the child is safe. The situation remains difficult; the update thanks people for their support.

The exchange

The upgrade changed course

Manánguri lists a 32 GB Corsair Vengeance LPX kit, two 16 GB DDR4-3600 modules, for A$249 in Australia. The seller bought it for an upgrade, then moved to a DDR5 motherboard instead.

A reader without an account

The Zapstore listing for Feeder offers a free Android feed reader with offline reading and OPML import and export. It runs locally and requires no account registration.

From the archive

WabiSabi, with the questions left in

Max shares an archival edit of Max Hillebrand’s WabiSabi presentation at Bitcoin Summer in Montreal in 2021.

The edit isolates the talk and audience questions from a six-hour livestream. The description covers Bitcoin’s privacy limitations, private digital cash and CoinJoin coordination.

The edit runs 53:37, with audience questions starting at 43:12. A return to a recorded explanation, with the surrounding conference sessions removed.
